messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kareem Nassar is a 54-year-old married man of Lebanese descent who works as a community organizer in a mid-sized American city, a role that has defined his sense of purpose for nearly two decades. He came to the intake appointment dressed in a long-sleeved shirt buttoned to the collar despite the warmth of the season, his movements careful and contained. He spoke quietly and with precision, pausing often, as though testing each word before releasing it.

The abuse he described had occurred over a period of approximately fourteen months in a relationship that preceded his current marriage, roughly a decade ago. His partner at the time had been someone he trusted completely — a person he had known for years before the relationship began, someone embedded in his social and professional world. The violence was not constant but episodic and escalating. The final and most severe incident took place at night, in the apartment they shared. He recalled the room being almost entirely dark when she came at him — he had been asleep, disoriented, and the first thing he registered was sound: her voice, then impact, then a helicopter passing low overhead through the open window, its rotors loud and rhythmic in the darkness. The beating left him with physical injuries and a fracture that required hospitalization. He told no one at the time what had actually happened.

In the weeks that followed, Kareem found that sleep had become unreliable in a way it had never been before. Fragments of that night returned to him without sequence or logic — the particular quality of her voice in the dark, the sound of the helicopter, the sensation of disorientation — arriving as disconnected pieces that he could not arrange into a coherent whole. More distressing still was how completely a moment in his surroundings could pull him back without warning. Walking to his car one evening, a helicopter passed overhead and he was, in his own words, suddenly there again — not remembering it, but inside it, the darkness and the sound indistinguishable from the present. He had to sit on the curb for several minutes before he could locate himself in the correct year.

He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt incontrovertible, that something in his own character had made this possible — that a man of genuine strength or discernment would never have been in that apartment, in that relationship, in that position. This belief sat alongside a broader collapse of assumptions he had carried into adulthood: that intimacy was fundamentally safe, that people who loved you did not destroy you, that the world operated according to recognizable moral principles. What had been most destabilizing was not the violence itself but the source of it — the betrayal by someone he had trusted at the level of his own survival. He had not found a way to reconstruct what he once believed.

In the years since, Kareem had quietly reorganized his life around the contours of what felt dangerous. He no longer passed through the neighborhood where the apartment had been, routing his commute several blocks out of the way without explaining this to his wife. His community organizing work requires him to attend evening meetings in church basements and community centers, and in those rooms he positions himself near exits and watches the door, scanning faces for signs of threat he cannot always name. He began wearing long sleeves and high collars year-round, finding in the concealment a form of control — if he was not visible, he could not be targeted. His wife had noticed the clothing and the detours and the watchfulness, and had asked questions he had deflected for years. The distance this had created between them had grown into something that now frightened him in its own right.

What finally brought Kareem to seek help was a moment at work three weeks prior. A colleague turned off the overhead lights in a meeting room to show a presentation, and Kareem left the room without speaking and did not return. He told his supervisor he had felt ill. He had not felt ill. He had felt that the darkness was going to kill him. He came to the first session hoping, above everything else, to become someone his wife could still reach.
